subject: history
subtitle: Skills and methods for investigating local history using evidence, maps, and community sources.

data.targetWord: the study of the past in a particular place or community — such as a town, village, street, school, mill, mine, or memorial — which connects everyday places to wider national and global history

examples.en-GB: A single street can show industrialisation, migration, class, gender, empire, poverty and reform through local history.

data.targetWord: a focused historical investigation built around a clear question — a good enquiry question invites explanation rather than just listing facts

examples.en-GB: A good enquiry question might be: How did the railway change this town between 1845 and 1901?

data.targetWord: a collection of historical records such as letters, maps, photographs, newspapers, census records, or council documents — archives often preserve official or powerful voices more than those of poorer communities

examples.en-GB: Local archives can include newspapers, census returns, school logbooks, and parish records.

data.targetWord: an official count of the population, recording names, ages, occupations, birthplaces, and households — useful for studying work, migration, and family structure in a local community

examples.en-GB: The 1851 census might show Irish migrants working as railway labourers in a local town.

data.targetWord: evidence from people's spoken memories, usually collected through interviews — valuable for personal experience but should be checked against other sources because memory can change

examples.en-GB: Oral history interviews with elderly residents can reveal details about a community that do not appear in written records.

data.targetWord: an object, building, or inscription created to remember a person, group, or event — memorials are selective, often leaving out causes, opponents, and missing groups

examples.en-GB: A war memorial might list soldiers' names but leave out the experiences of families, colonised peoples, or opponents of the war.

data.targetWord: the growth of machine-based production, factories, mines, mills, and transport networks — it affected local communities through new jobs, migration, housing, and pollution

examples.en-GB: Industrialisation brought a railway station, factory jobs, and rows of workers' cottages to many local towns in the nineteenth century.

data.targetWord: the growth of towns and cities as people moved from rural areas for factory work, creating crowded housing, pollution, and pressure on sanitation

examples.en-GB: Urbanisation in the nineteenth century meant that many English towns grew rapidly as factories attracted workers.

data.targetWord: the movement of people from one place to another — in the nineteenth century, people moved to towns for factory work, and migrants from Ireland and Wales moved to industrial areas

examples.en-GB: Census birthplaces showing people from County Cork and Wales in a mill town are evidence of migration patterns.

data.targetWord: a group of territories controlled by one country — in local history, empire can be visible through imported goods (tea, sugar, cotton), street names, memorials to imperial wars, and merchant wealth

examples.en-GB: A shop advertising tea, sugar and tobacco shows how local consumers were connected to global trade routes and colonial production.

data.targetWord: something that stays the same over time — in local history, older churches, street patterns, and market routes may continue while other features change around them

examples.en-GB: The parish church appearing on both an 1850 map and a modern map is evidence of continuity in the townscape.

data.targetWord: something that becomes different over time — in local history, the arrival of a railway, the growth of factories, or the building of new housing are all examples of change

examples.en-GB: The arrival of a railway station is evidence of change in a local town's transport and economy.

data.targetWord: information about where a source comes from — who made it, when, why, and for whom — which helps historians judge how useful and reliable it is

examples.en-GB: A local newspaper's provenance matters because it may represent the views of literate, wealthier or politically active groups.

data.targetWord: a change intended to improve a law, institution, or society — in nineteenth-century Britain, reform included the widening of voting rights through Acts in 1832, 1867, and 1884

examples.en-GB: A local reform meeting in 1868 connects to the national Second Reform Act of 1867, which extended voting rights.

data.targetWord: a system in which people have political power through voting and representation — in Victorian Britain, democracy widened slowly through reform acts, though most women could not vote until the twentieth century

examples.en-GB: In 1832, the First Reform Act widened the vote for some middle-class men, but most adults still could not vote.

data.targetWord: a building created in industrial towns to provide adult education, self-improvement, and civic life — evidence of civic pride and the growth of working-class learning in the Victorian period

examples.en-GB: A mechanics' institute on a local map suggests the town valued adult education and civic improvement.

data.targetWord: a movement in the 1830s-1840s that demanded wider male suffrage, secret ballots, and other political reforms — local Chartist meetings show communities debating national democratic change

examples.en-GB: Local newspaper reports of Chartist meetings in the 1840s connect the local community to national democratic demands.

data.targetWord: an institution where people who could not support themselves were housed and made to work — created by the New Poor Law of 1834, and visible on Victorian maps as evidence of poverty management

examples.en-GB: A workhouse on a Victorian map of a local town is evidence of how poverty was managed under the New Poor Law.

data.targetWord: comparing old and modern maps to identify what changed (new buildings, roads, railways) and what stayed the same (church, river, street pattern) in a local area over time

examples.en-GB: Comparing an 1850 map with a modern one might show that fields became housing while the church and river remained.

data.targetWord: a group of people connected by place, identity, work, religion, family, culture, or shared experience — local history helps us understand how different communities experienced wider historical change

examples.en-GB: A census can reveal a diverse community, showing migrants, factory workers, domestic servants, and canal workers living in one street.

data.targetWord: people whose experiences are not recorded in surviving historical sources — including poorer people, women, children, migrants, and colonised peoples who may be harder to trace in archives

examples.en-GB: A war memorial may list officers' names but leave out working-class soldiers, women, and civilians — these are missing voices.

data.targetWord: an artificial waterway built to transport goods such as coal, cotton, and grain between towns and ports — canals were an early part of the Industrial Revolution before railways became dominant

examples.en-GB: A canal wharf on an 1850 map shows that a local town was connected to industrial trade routes before the railway arrived.

data.targetWord: the use of children as workers in factories, mines, and workshops — evidence of it can be found in census data showing young ages for workers, and factory inspection reports

examples.en-GB: A census entry for a 13-year-old factory piecer is evidence of child labour in a Victorian mill town.

data.targetWord: the historical importance of a person, event, or development — judged using criteria such as the number of people affected, depth of impact, duration, and links to wider history

examples.en-GB: The arrival of a railway was significant for a local town because it connected it to national markets and created new jobs.

data.targetWord: a later explanation of the past — in local history, different historians, museums, local residents, or family historians may interpret the same local evidence differently depending on their questions and values

examples.en-GB: One interpretation of Victorian change might focus on progress through railways and schools, while another focuses on the hardship of child labour and overcrowding.

data.title: Steps to evaluate a historical source in a local history enquiry
items: Identify what the source says or shows (content)
Work out what can be inferred from it
Consider who made it, when, why, and for whom (provenance)
Think about what was happening at the time (context)
Explain how it helps answer the enquiry question (usefulness)

data.title: Chain of cause and consequence: Industrial growth in a local town
items: Industrial growth brings mills, mines, workshops, and warehouses
More jobs attract workers and create migration
Population growth leads to new housing, schools, chapels, and shops
Pressure builds on sanitation, wages, and local government
Reform campaigns push for improvements in living and political conditions

data.title: Key stages of democratic reform affecting local communities, in order
items: First Reform Act widens the vote for some middle-class men (1832)
Second Reform Act extends the vote to more working-class men in towns (1867)
Third Reform Act extends the vote to many rural working men (1884)
